To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the peritoneal and circulating immune responses after laparoscoic surgery are dependent on the type of gas used for insufflation and the exposure of the peritoneum to air.
factors in circulating air may induce lipopolysac-charide translocation across the gastrointestinal tract, and subsequent stimulation of the postoperative immune responses.
factors in circulating air can cause translocation of gut-derived LPS into the peritoneum and subsequent stimulation of peritoneal and circulating immune cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the surgical environment on the postoperative immune response.
the effect of air contamination of the abdominal cavity on immune responses after laparos-copy.
the role of air as a mediator of the immune response to surgery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

exposure of the peritoneum to air, as occurs in laparotomy, is associated with a more pronounced immune response than that observed with carbon dioxide laparascopy, which is associated with less air exposure.
exposure of the peritoneum to air, as occurs during laparoscopy, is associated with a significant inflammatory response and LPS translocation.
exposure of the peritoneum to air, rather than the surgical technique, may be the most important determinant of early postoperative inflammation and immune responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of carbon dioxide for insufflation in laparoscopic surgery has the potential to reduce the systemic inflammatory response and may reduce the risk of postoperative infections.

the exposure of the peritoneum to air during laparoscopic surgery results in a systemic inflammatory response, which may be due to gut‐derived lipolysaccharide translocation across the intestinal mucosa.
the exposure of the peritoneum to air induces gut-derived LPS translocation across gut mucosal barriers, which results in a pro-inflammatory immune response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
exposure of the peritoneum to air can stimulate the release of inflammatory mediators from the peritoneum.
the use of air in laparoscopy may be associated with increased postoperative immune responses and LPS translocation across an intact gut.
exposure of the peritoneum to air can stimulate an inflammatory response that is not seen with laparoscopy using carbon dioxide.
